statements.text: You also said in the advanced policy questions, and in your testimony, that we must invest in artificial intelligence and machine-learning platforms and programs to increase our ability to detect, defend, and respond to conventional Iranian military capabilities. [...] we do a quarterly exercise that uses artificial intelligence for target detection. [...] It culminated in a Marine F-35 dropping a live, thousand-pound bomb on an artificially intelligence-derived grid that was one meter off from the surveyed grid.
statements.context: Senate Armed Services Committee confirmation hearing for LTG Kurilla as CENTCOM commander.

statements.text: If I am confirmed, I would work with the team at DOD OIG to ensure that we are at the forefront in addressing the use of emerging technologies across the DOD [...] I have been pleased to serve for several years now as the Vice Chair of the CIGIE Technology Committee and as the Chair of the Emerging Technology Subcommittee [...] I am aware that the DOD OIG has been active in this area, including partnering with my office at NSA OIG on an ongoing joint evaluation of the integration of artificial intelligence in signals intelligence activities at the NSA.
statements.context: Written responses to Senate Armed Services Committee advance policy questions for the nomination of Honorable Robert P. Storch as DOD Inspector General.

statements.text: Acting on the guidance of the Deputy Secretary of Defense and recommendations from the National Security Commission on AI, USSTRATCOM implemented the Command Data and AI Center (CDAI) to solve the command's most intractable problems through the application of advanced AI/ML methods. [...] We will do this in ways consistent with the DOD Ethical Principles for Artificial Intelligence, while continuing to lead in developing best practices for the development and application of AI and ML technologies to ensure their use is safe, secure, reliable, and consistent with our values.
statements.context: Written testimony submitted to the Senate Armed Services Committee for the FY 2023 Department of Defense authorization request, covering USSTRATCOM priorities including nuclear deterrence and NC3 modernization.

statements.text: As the ubiquity of data and speed of decisionmaking continue to increase, Allies and adversaries alike could feel pressure to delegate key decisionmaking functions to machines, which could produce unpredictable results if systems are not appropriately designed, tested, and used. [...] For example, in February the United States announced a Political Declaration on the Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Military Domain that creates strong norms surrounding the development and use of AI and autonomy in all military systems. It reiterates the commitment we publicized in our Nuclear Posture Review to have a human ``in the loop'' for all actions critical to informing and executing decisions by the President to initiate and terminate nuclear weapon employment.
statements.context: Written question-for-the-record submitted by Senator Manchin to General Cotton during the FY2024 DOD authorization hearings, asking how AI and other novel technologies affect the nuclear risk environment.

statements.text: PRC leaders remain focused on using both licit and illicit means to seize a dominant position in critical and emerging dual-use technology sectors—artificial intelligence, advanced robotics, quantum technologies, directed energy, and hypersonic systems—and using that dominant position to advance their authoritarian agenda. To increase adoption of PRC developed technology, the PRC is pursuing acceptance of its national technology standards across the globe.
statements.context: Written statement submitted to the Senate Armed Services Committee for the FY 2024 Department of Defense authorization request, covering USEUCOM threat assessments.

statements.text: We seek to set the gold standard for data-driven decisionmaking for our Service-like and Combatant Command responsibilities—focusing on the talent, architecture, and processes needed to capitalize on data and artificial intelligence (AI)-related technologies.
statements.context: Statement before the Senate Armed Services Committee on the FY 2024 Defense Authorization Request, discussing USSOCOM modernization and data-driven technology adoption.

statements.text: In the coming years, developments in new technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI), quantum computing, and additive manufacturing will continue to disrupt the way war is conducted. [...] As AI and other disruptive technologies rapidly proliferate, we must proactively work to gain every advantage. [...] Our application of AI solutions will provide our forces with decision superiority as we map, measure, manage, and govern the battle space.
statements.context: Statement by the Chief of Naval Operations before the Senate Armed Services Committee on the FY 2024 defense budget request.

statements.text: Do you have any concerns that AI will disrupt our life dramatically, and that there are steps that we should start contemplating now?
statements.context: Senate Armed Services Committee Worldwide Threats hearing; Chairman Reed questions Director of National Intelligence Avril Haines on AI disruption.

statements.text: When you have the proponents of AI warning us this week that AI could be the catastrophic destruction of our species, well, guess where that is going to be first manifested—in the military domain, I believe.
statements.context: Senate floor remarks during a debate on military officer promotions held up by Senator Tuberville's protest over reproductive healthcare policy.

statements.text: We need a multilateral approach. We need an export regime with our allies, similar to the CFIUS process, which has grown and developed.
statements.context: Senate Banking Committee hearing on national security challenges in emerging technology, during the Q&A portion with expert witnesses.

statements.text: The fiscal year 2025 budget prioritizes artificial intelligence (AI), investing $1.8 billion in research, development, test, and evaluation funds and in operations and maintenance funds, highlighting the strategic importance of AI to our Joint Force for both the near-and long-term.
statements.context: Senate Armed Services Committee hearing on the Department of Defense Authorization for Appropriations for Fiscal Year 2025, covering nuclear modernization, digital innovation, and defense industrial base investments.

statements.text: Finally, we project that both the PRC and Russia will use artificial intelligence to develop autonomous cyber weapon systems to optimize offensive cyber operations.
statements.context: Written testimony submitted to the Senate Armed Services Committee for the FY 2025 National Defense Authorization Act.

statements.text: each day we see news stories about the rise of AI, as well as stories about our adversaries exploiting the technology for bad. What are you doing in the AI space? How do you assess our capabilities against the PRC? [...] The PRC has rapidly adopted Al for domestic surveillance and military applications, and Al has the potential to dramatically expand their malicious cyber activities, posing an increasing threat that is not bound by the rule of law.
statements.context: Written questions for the record submitted to General Haugh (CYBERCOM Commander) during a Senate Armed Services Committee hearing on the FY2025 National Defense Authorization Act.

statements.text: Stormbreaker, an AI-based gaming and simulation capability.
statements.context: Written questions for the record submitted during the Senate Armed Services Committee's hearing on DOD authorization for FY2025, with Senator King questioning Admiral Aquilino on AI and data investments.

statements.text: I think the issue is that we have seen some calls for things like a Federal agency that would license large language models. It would not be surprising that the companies that will be able to achieve those licenses will just happen to be companies that state their value in trillions of dollars versus small and medium sized businesses.
statements.context: Remarks delivered during a panel or hearing titled "The Need to Protect Americans' Privacy and the AI Accelerant."

statements.text: So our global competitiveness is absolutely impacted if we restrict the access to the technology that drives us forward.
statements.context: Remarks delivered during a US congressional hearing on privacy and AI.

statements.text: Well, thank you for the question and, of course, that is the normal behavior of any company that has significant compliance resources is to look for ways to make sure that they are prepared to comply. [...] But I think we should look through the lens of harms to make the choices that Congress has to make.
statements.context: Witness testimony before a congressional hearing on privacy and AI, responding to a question about corporate compliance behavior and AI regulation.

statements.text: Well, as I touched on earlier, I think licensing regime always leads to a situation where those with the power and the time and the number of lawyers to go through the process of meeting that licensing requirement are the ones who win at the table rather than those that have the best technology or the best ideas. So I am always concerned about a licensing regime that is the only door into success.
statements.context: Panel discussion on AI and privacy, titled "The Need to Protect Americans' Privacy and the AI Accelerant," before a congressional committee.

statements.text: In recent years, regional TCOs have expanded their sources of revenue and leveraged new technology such as drones and artificial intelligence, almost certainly to increase their resilience. This has allowed regional TCOs to amass levels of power that directly threaten local citizens, regional governments, and the United States.
statements.context: Written responses to Senate Armed Services Committee policy questions for the nomination of Stephen A. Feinberg as Deputy Secretary of Defense.

statements.text: We believe it is necessary to require tech companies, not American families, to foot the bill for their load. [...] As the ones who stand to benefit most, the multi-billion-dollar AI industry should be responsible for these costs.
statements.venue: Joint letter from New England senators (including Reed) to ISO New England on AI data centers

statements.text: President Trump is dead wrong. His shortsighted view increases the likelihood that AI will be misused by bad actors or unsafely sped up by corporate interests at the expense of the public.
statements.venue: Reed press release on Trump and AI guardrails

statements.text: Artificial Intelligence is a powerful tool that offers opportunities and risks. As with any new technology, especially something as cutting-edge and revolutionary as AI, laws and regulations must keep pace with the tech’s capabilities. Congress must do its job and provide balanced oversight, standards, and rules of the road.
statements.venue: Reed press release on Trump and AI guardrails

statements.text: Adding some brakes and speed limits to AI development does not have to mean losing pace with the Chinese. That excuse is both a failure of imagination and a failure of leadership and misunderstands the nature of the AI race itself.
statements.venue: Reed press release on Trump and AI guardrails

statements.text: Consumers deserve transparent pricing and equal treatment, not hidden technology that misuses their personal data to set different prices for the same item and charge some shoppers more than others. AI is a powerful tool, but it presents real and pressing challenges. This is one of them and Congress needs to take thoughtful, concrete steps to ban exploitative AI-enabled price discrimination and ensure fairness in the marketplace.
statements.venue: Reed press release on AI-enabled price discrimination
